walkthroughs.body_html: Habitat fragmentation increases edge effects and isolates populations, reducing gene flow and increasing inbreeding. Small patches support fewer species and are vulnerable to local extinctions. Roads, fields and urban areas create barriers. The species-area relationship predicts that halving habitat area typically loses around 10 percent of species.

Wildlife corridors such as hedgerows, river margins, green bridges over motorways and underpasses link isolated patches. They allow movement for feeding, mating and seasonal migration, maintaining gene flow and resilience. Examples include the European Green Belt and the Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative across North America.

Rewilding restores ecological processes, often by reintroducing keystone species. Wolves to Yellowstone (1995) reshaped vegetation and rivers via trophic cascades. Beavers returned to Devon are reducing flood peaks and increasing biodiversity. Rewilding contrasts with traditional management by stepping back and letting ecosystems self-regulate.
